seoTitle: MIC and Zone of Inhibition Calculator — Formula & Results
seoDesc: Convert a measured zone of inhibition into a minimum inhibitory concentration, and work out how much of it you actually achieved. Free mic and zone of inhibit
h1: MIC and Zone of Inhibition Calculator
summary:
Convert a measured zone of inhibition into a minimum inhibitory concentration, and work out how much of it you actually achieved. It returns zone per log₂ MIC, estimated MIC, susceptibility ratio and drug concentration in the well, and the panel shows all of them at once.

The zone diameter falls roughly linearly with the log of the MIC, so two calibration points from a known strain are enough to read an unknown one. Press Calculate and the results appear in the grey boxes; after the first press they keep up with every edit, so there is no page to reload. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the MIC and Zone of Inhibition
sections.html:
MIC = MIC_ref × 2^((Zone_ref − Zone) ÷ slope), with slope = (Zone_ref − Zone_lo) ÷ log₂(MIC_lo ÷ MIC_ref). Concentration in a well (µg/mL) = disc µg ÷ volume (mL)

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
MICminimum inhibitory concentrationµg/mL
zonediameter of the clear ring around the discmm
breakpointthe MIC above which the organism is called resistantµg/mL

sections.title: How do I use the MIC and Zone of Inhibition?
sections.html:
Every input sits in the same order the formula is written, so the page reads like the equation.

  1. Measure the clear zone around the disc in millimetres.
  2. Enter the two calibration points from a reference strain and the breakpoint for the organism.
  3. Read the estimated MIC and whether it sits above or below the breakpoint.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: zone of inhibition of 22 mm, antibiotic per disc of 30 µg, calibration zone, low mic of 25 mm, reference mic for that zone of 1 µg/mL, calibration zone, high mic of 15 mm, reference mic for that zone of 8 µg/mL, breakpoint mic of 4 µg/mL, well volume of 200 µL.

Substituting them into the formula gives zone per log₂ mic of 3.33 mm, estimated mic of 1.87 µg/mL, susceptibility ratio of 0.4665 ×, drug concentration in the well of 150 µg/mL.

Those numbers come from the same solver the page runs in your browser, not from an illustration, so typing different inputs moves the answer exactly as the arithmetic says.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
The number on its own is not a judgement. These are the bands most often used when the result is quoted in a paper, a report or a label:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
ratio under 0.5Susceptiblethe drug works at a normal dose
ratio 0.5 – 2Intermediateclose to the breakpoint; check the method
ratio above 2Resistantthe MIC exceeds the breakpoint

  • The relationship is logarithmic, not linear: doubling the MIC changes the zone by a fixed number of millimetres, set by the drug's diffusion through the agar.

  • Zone size depends on the agar depth, the inoculum density and the diffusion rate of the drug, which is why the calibration points must come from the same protocol.

  • MIC is a laboratory value. Whether a dose works in a patient also depends on protein binding, tissue penetration and the drug's pharmacokinetics.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
These are the errors that account for almost every wrong answer people bring to this calculator:

  • Measuring the disc itself as well as the zone, or reading the zone with a ruler laid across the wrong axis.
  • Comparing zones from different media — Mueller-Hinton is the standard for a reason.
  • Calling an organism resistant from a zone alone without the breakpoint table for that species.

Bacterial growth curve. Enzyme activity. Specific growth rate.

faq.q: What does a 20 mm zone mean?
faq.a: It depends on the drug and the disc load: for a 30 µg disc of a well-diffusing antibiotic it usually means susceptible.
Because diffusion creates a concentration gradient, and the zone edge marks the concentration equal to the MIC — a log relationship.

faq.q: Can I use this for fungi?
faq.a: Yes, with antifungal discs and the species-appropriate breakpoints.

faq.q: What does the MIC and Zone of Inhibition actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns zone per log₂ MIC, estimated MIC, susceptibility ratio and drug concentration in the well. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
